tasks.registered_metrics_text:
a) Define the metric(s) to assess a property of an algorithm. These metrics should reflect the desired algorithm
properties described in assessment aim(s) (see above). State which metric(s) were used to compute the ranking(s) (if
any).
  • Example 1: Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC)
  • Example 2: Area under curve (AUC)
Mean accuracy over several few-shot task instances. The sampled few-shot tasks will include different numbers of
shots, i.e. examples per class. Since we believe that a range of 3 to 10 shots is the most relevant for our application,
we include this range in the ranking.

b) Justify why the metric(s) was/were chosen, preferably with reference to the biomedical application.

Since we are trying to assess the few-shot classification capabilities and sample few-shot tasks with balanced
classes (n examples per class), measuring accuracy is equivalent to measuring AUC and a sufficiently informative
metric. The accuracy must be measured over several tasks to reduce bias.





 MICCAI Learn2Learn Challenge
tasks.registered_ranking_text:
a) Describe the method used to compute a performance rank for all submitted algorithms based on the generated
metric results on the test cases. Typically the text will describe how results obtained per case and metric are aggregated
to arrive at a final score/ranking.

For each submission, the accuracies of all sampled few-shot instances of each test task are averaged. These average
accuracies are used to genrate rankings for each task. These rankings are averaged to generate a final aggregate
challenge ranking. We use this rank-then-aggregate approach to not implicitly weigh any tasks higher than others.

b) Describe the method(s) used to manage submissions with missing results on test cases.

The participants will submit algorithms as Docker containers.
For the validation phase on grand-challenge.org, a time limit of 2 minutes applies for each test case, i.e. each of the
single few-shot instances per N and task. Failed submissions or submissions that have timed out will return an
error. This will allow the participants to test the validity of their submission.


For the final evaluation and ranking, we will download the submitted Docker containers and execute them on our
local hardware. The final evaluation will encompass 100 few-shot task instances per N and task.
An execution time limit of 2 minutes and 30 seconds per test case, i.e. per few-shot instance, will apply. The
additional 30 seconds should provide ample margin of error for all algorithms that have passed validation to
complete the final evaluation. Stopped or failed predictions will be integrated in the final ranking as if generated
by a random classifier, e.g. an accuracy of 0.2 for a 5-way multi-class problem.

c) Justify why the described ranking scheme(s) was/were used.

Not applicable.

registered_task_submissions.protocol_description: Participating teams are expected to submit their algorithms as a Docker container. The container should be able to accept a few-shot task instance, containing a support set of labelled images and a query set of unlabelled images, and output predictions for the query set. The submitted algorithms will be run on the challenge servers using a public set of validation tasks with a fixed execution time limit of 20 minutes. Based on our preliminary baseline experiments, a time limit of 2 minutes per few-shot task instance will allow even complex algorithms to finish execution. The docker containers should be self-contained and include the model used for the few-shot training process and the predictions, since we can not guarantee access to the internet for the containers at runtime. In particular, it is not possible to download models or any other additional data during container execution. The container size limit is 8GB. The online validation will allow us to publish a preliminary leaderboard and allow participants to check their algorithm for validity and compatibility with our evaluation code. As the latter is the online validation’s main purpose, the number of few-shot instances used is limited to one per dataset and per N. This keeps computational costs reasonable, while allowing a substantial number of validation submissions per team. However, participating teams are still able to additionally produce as many few-shot instances as they wish from the publicly available validation set using our published evaluation code and validate their algorithms on their own hardware before submission. For the final testing stage, we will download the Docker containers and evaluate them locally on our hardware. The final evaluation will encompass more test cases. We will adjust the execution time limit to 2 minutes and 30 seconds per few-shot instance, to provide a generous margin of error for all algorithms that have passed validation to complete the final evaluation. Participating teams are allowed to select up to three submissions as final, of which the best-performing one will be used for the team’s ranking. After the submission deadline for results, participating teams will submit a short report of one to three pages describing their algorithm. The report should contain a brief description of the methods used in the three final submissions, including the model, the data used for training and hyperparameter settings. Teams are required to also include a link to their code to ensure the reproducibility of their method. MICCAI Learn2Learn Challenge
